latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bloodstream organisms seed the vascular synovium and enter a joint space that has limited local host clearance. This is common with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, catheter infection, skin infection, endocarditis, urinary or gastrointestinal bacteremia, and disseminated gonococcal disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Direct inoculation or contiguous spread into joint
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Joint infection begins from penetrating trauma, bite, intra-articular injection, arthroscopy, surgery, adjacent cellulitis, osteomyelitis, or abscess extension rather than a primary bloodstream event.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Prosthetic joint biofilm and implant-adjacent infection
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Organisms adhere to prosthetic material or cement, form biofilm, and sustain infection around the implant, adjacent synovium, soft tissue, and bone. This mechanism makes source control and prolonged active therapy more important than in uncomplicated native joint infection.

Replicating organisms in synovial fluid and synovium drive purulence, synovitis, high synovial neutrophils, positive cultures, and ongoing inflammatory damage until active antibiotics and drainage reduce the burden.
Innate immune activation recruits neutrophils into synovial fluid, producing painful tense effusion, warmth, swelling, restricted range of motion, and high CRP or ESR.

Bacterial products, neutrophil enzymes, cytokines, and pressure from purulent effusion damage cartilage, subchondral bone, and periarticular structures, creating erosions, joint space loss, instability, and long-term functional loss.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Periarticular abscess, osteomyelitis, and deep extension
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Infection escapes the joint capsule or extends into adjacent bone and soft tissue, producing periarticular abscess, osteomyelitis, chest wall or mediastinal spread from sternoclavicular disease, iliopsoas abscess from sacroiliac disease, or sinus tract around prosthetic joints.

Joint infection or associated bacteremia drives IL-1, IL-6, TNF, CRP, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, procalcitonin, malaise, and rigors. Fever and leukocytosis may be muted in elderly or immunosuppressed patients.

Joint infection may be seeded by bacteremia or become a sustained focus for bacteremia, increasing risk of endocarditis, septic pulmonary or systemic emboli, vertebral osteomyelitis, epidural abscess, and infection of other joints.
Purulent effusion, loculated joint infection, abscess, infected prosthesis, sinus tract, or untreated hematogenous source continues to feed bacterial burden despite antibiotics.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Septic organ dysfunction from joint infection
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: High bacterial burden, bacteremia, cytokine release, vasoplegia, capillary leak, and hypoperfusion produce hypotension, lactate rise, AKI, respiratory failure, encephalopathy, and high short-term mortality.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Synovium is highly vascular and can be seeded during bacteremia.
Direct entry or adjacent infection places viable organisms into the joint space.
Biofilm on prosthetic material continuously sheds organisms into peri-implant tissue and synovial fluid.
Bacterial PAMPs and complement activation rapidly recruit neutrophils into synovium and fluid.
Neutrophil enzymes, cytokines, and pressure damage cartilage and subchondral bone.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Most prominent with S. aureus, streptococci, gram-negative bacilli, endovascular infection, prosthetic infection, or delayed drainage.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: A high-burden joint focus can seed the bloodstream, and bacteremia can seed additional sites.
Persistent bacteremia can seed other native or prosthetic joints.
Capsular and bony damage allows infection to extend into adjacent bone or soft tissue.
Abscess, osteomyelitis, or sinus tract are less likely to sterilize without drainage or debridement.
Undrained fluid, infected hardware, or an untreated source sustains viable bacterial burden.
Persistent source maintains antigen release and acute-phase response.
Systemic inflammatory response can progress to vasoplegia and organ dysfunction.
Purulent synovitis creates the core inflamed-joint clinical phenotype.
Capsular distension and synovial inflammation cause severe joint pain.
Effusion and periarticular inflammation produce swelling.
Local hyperemia and inflammation create warmth.
Superficial joints often show overlying erythema; deep joints may not.
Synovial inflammation makes passive and active motion painful.
Pain and effusion limit movement.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Applies mainly to hip, knee, ankle, foot, or sacroiliac involvement.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Lower-extremity joint pain and effusion impair ambulation.
Bacteremia can seed multiple joints, especially in immunosuppression, rheumatoid arthritis, dialysis, or endocarditis.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk rises with bacteremia, injection drug use, hemodialysis access, diabetes, and immunosuppression, but can occur without recognized risk factors.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: The sternoclavicular joint is usually infected through hematogenous spread.
A prosthetic implant allows biofilm persistence and late relapse risk.
Peri-implant infection can loosen hardware and compromise implant function.
Purulent synovitis often creates fluid that can be aspirated or washed out.
Ultrasound, CT, or MRI may show effusion in the involved joint.
Inflammation extends into adjacent fat, muscle, capsule, and soft tissue.
A recent joint procedure, injection, or trauma identifies an inoculation route.
Erosions and cortical destruction appear when infection damages adjacent bone.
Cartilage injury can progress rapidly if bacterial burden and inflammation persist.
Cartilage destruction, instability, and periarticular damage can leave long-term disability.
Capsular rupture or adjacent soft-tissue infection can form abscess.
Adjacent bone can become infected from a joint focus or be the source that extends into the joint.
Hematogenous septic arthritis often coexists with positive blood cultures.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Especially important with S. aureus bacteremia, persistent bacteremia, prosthetic material, dialysis catheter, injection drug use, or embolic phenomena.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bacteremia from or to a joint can involve cardiac valves.
Endocarditis or septic thrombophlebitis can produce pulmonary or systemic septic emboli.
Purulent fluid, abscess, infected hardware, or hematogenous source increases need for drainage or source removal.
Persistent source means current source control is inadequate.
Bacteremia or remote infection makes hematogenous seeding more likely.
Dialysis catheters and other endovascular devices can cause bacteremia that seeds joints.
Cytokines raise hypothalamic set-point, though fever may be absent.
Fever, pain, and systemic inflammation drive tachycardia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: May be low or normal with neutropenia, immunosuppression, older age, or indolent organisms.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Acute bacterial inflammation usually raises circulating leukocytes.
IL-6-driven acute phase response raises CRP and tracks response.
Inflammation increases fibrinogen and ESR, with slower kinetics than CRP.
Septic vasodilation and capillary leak reduce perfusion pressure.
ARDS, septic emboli, pneumonia, or volume overload may reduce oxygenation.
Hypoperfusion and adrenergic stress increase lactate.
Septic hypoperfusion and nephrotoxic exposures can cause AKI.
Septic organ dysfunction can progress to shock without active therapy and source control.
Shock, inflammation, and antibiotic toxicity risk raise AKI hazard.
Mortality is driven mainly by sepsis, organ dysfunction, uncontrolled source, and severe comorbidity.
Joint destruction creates the structural basis for chronic pain and reduced function.
Sustained bacteremia is a major route to valve infection.
Endocarditis vegetations can embolize to lung or systemic circulation.
Shock sharply increases short-term mortality risk.

Frequently elevated with slower rise and fall than CRP.
May rise with bacteremia or septic shock; can be low in localized or indolent infection.
Usually normal in localized disease and elevated in hypoperfusion, shock, or severe sepsis.
May be elevated from baseline CKD, dialysis context, sepsis-associated AKI, or nephrotoxic therapy.
Can be high from AKI, CKD, dehydration, obstructive uropathy, or dialysis context.
Usually nonspecific; may fall with severe sepsis, DIC, marrow suppression, or baseline hematologic disease.
Parent finding for a joint with acute pain, swelling, warmth, restricted motion, or drainage suggesting intra-articular infection.
Severe focal pain is typical, but indolent organisms or prosthetic infection can be less dramatic.
Effusion and periarticular edema create visible or palpable swelling.
Warmth is common in superficial joints and may be hard to assess in hip, sacroiliac, spine-adjacent, or deep prosthetic infection.
Erythema is common over superficial joints or associated cellulitis, and may be absent with deep joints or indolent organisms.
Pain with active or passive motion is one of the most useful bedside features.
Range of motion is limited by pain, effusion, and capsular inflammation.
Lower-extremity septic arthritis can cause inability to walk or bear weight.
Extent of multiple infected or clinically involved joints; higher values fit bacteremia, endocarditis, rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, and dialysis contexts.
Captures the specific sternoclavicular pattern, which can present as chest wall or shoulder pain with swelling near the clavicle.
Presence of an arthroplasty or other prosthetic joint material in the infected joint.
Purulent discharge, wound dehiscence, or sinus tract around a native or prosthetic joint suggests a high-burden draining focus.
Recent arthrocentesis, injection, arthroscopy, arthroplasty, trauma, or surgery can provide direct inoculation.
Probability that the involved joint contains fluid or pus accessible to aspiration, arthroscopy, open washout, or image-guided drainage.
Ultrasound, CT, MRI, or radiograph evidence of effusion, joint fluid, or intra-articular collection.
Imaging or exam evidence of soft-tissue swelling, fat stranding, myositis, cellulitis, or capsular edema around the infected joint.
Gas within a joint or adjacent wound can indicate open communication, gas-forming infection, recent surgery, or prosthetic joint infection.
CT, MRI, radiograph, or operative evidence of cortical erosion, subchondral destruction, clavicular/manubrial erosion, or adjacent bone damage.
Estimated activity of biofilm-mediated peri-implant infection.
Radiographic, operative, or functional evidence that an infected implant is loose or failing.
Need for aspiration, washout, debridement, implant management, abscess drainage, or control of a hematogenous source.
Adequacy of drainage, washout, prosthetic management, abscess control, and removal or treatment of any bacteremic source.
Probability that the joint was seeded from bloodstream infection rather than direct inoculation.
Probability that a dialysis catheter, central line, endovascular device, or endocarditis source is driving bacteremia and joint seeding.
Etiologic probability for S. aureus, which is common in native and prosthetic septic arthritis and strongly linked to bacteremia.
Probability that S. aureus is methicillin-resistant, shaped by prior MRSA, healthcare exposure, dialysis, injection drug use, local epidemiology, and cultures.
Probability of streptococcal disease, including pneumococcal, beta-hemolytic, viridans, and group G streptococci.
Probability of Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas, Salmonella, Pasteurella, or other gram-negative bacilli, shaped by age, urinary or GI source, immunosuppression, trauma, bites, or prosthetic infection.
Probability of disseminated gonococcal arthritis, shaped by sexual exposure, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and mucosal NAAT evidence.
Probability of anaerobes or Cutibacterium-type indolent infection, especially with shoulder/prosthetic surgery, delayed culture growth, bite or oral source, or low-grade presentation.
Probability that the current antibiotic regimen is active against the causative organism and reaches the joint or peri-implant infection.
Probability that a staphylococcal isolate is susceptible to anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam therapy such as cefazolin or nafcillin.
Probability that gram-positive septic arthritis pathogen is susceptible to vancomycin.
Hazard of concurrent or persistent bloodstream infection related to the joint infection or its source.
Hazard that bacteremia associated with septic arthritis involves cardiac valves.
Hazard of pulmonary or systemic septic emboli from endocarditis, septic thrombosis, or sustained bacteremia.
Hazard of abscess around the joint or tracking into nearby deep spaces.
Hazard of adjacent osteomyelitis from or into the infected joint.
Hazard of irreversible cartilage, bone, ligament, or implant-adjacent structural damage.
Hazard of chronic pain, reduced range of motion, joint instability, need for reconstruction, or persistent disability.
Hazard of progression to septic shock from uncontrolled joint infection or associated bacteremia.
Hazard of AKI from sepsis, shock, baseline kidney disease, obstruction, or nephrotoxic antimicrobials.
Hazard of ARDS or severe respiratory failure in septic shock, septic emboli, pneumonia, or high inflammatory burden.

Disease-specific lifespan hazard driven by septic shock, persistent bacteremia, endocarditis, severe comorbidity, delayed source control, prosthetic infection, and frailty rather than by local joint pain alone.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Effective drainage or implant/source management usually allows CRP to fall after active antimicrobial therapy.
Fever often improves after drainage plus active antibiotics.
Purulent drainable effusion creates an immediate source-control target.
Infected prosthetic material often requires debridement, liner exchange, staged revision, or suppressive strategy.
Persistent bacteremia can infect valves, especially with S. aureus.
Valve vegetations can embolize to pulmonary or systemic sites.
Structural joint damage drives chronic pain, stiffness, instability, and reconstruction need.
Bone destruction on imaging raises concern for adjacent osteomyelitis.
Shock is a major driver of short-term death.
Pain and reduced motion are linked bedside manifestations of synovitis.
Effusion and capsular pressure amplify motion pain.
Both reflect systemic inflammation, with ESR usually moving more slowly.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vancomycin component protects against MRSA while cultures are pending.
Additional beta-lactam coverage matters with urinary, GI, bite, immunosuppressed, healthcare, or prosthetic contexts.
The antimicrobial vector field should shrink when the regimen is inactive against the true organism.
Renal impairment changes dosing and nephrotoxicity risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Vancomycin and broad beta-lactam exposure can increase AKI risk, especially with baseline kidney injury.

treatments.context_specific_role: Initial active coverage while cultures, source, prosthetic status, and severity are clarified.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cefazolin or nafcillin-like therapy is strongest when MSSA susceptibility is established.
Methicillin resistance removes the core beta-lactam effect.
Persistent pus or hardware biofilm reduces antimicrobial-only success.

side_effects.interpretation: Rash or infusion reactions can mimic inflammatory skin findings but do not explain the joint source.

treatments.context_specific_role: Culture-directed therapy for MSSA septic arthritis and associated bacteremia after susceptibility is known.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: MRSA-active therapy is necessary when MRSA probability or culture evidence is high.
Vancomycin effect is reduced if susceptibility or exposure is poor; alternative MRSA-active agents may be needed.
Renal dysfunction affects vancomycin exposure and toxicity.

side_effects.interpretation: Vancomycin exposure can increase nephrotoxicity hazard.

treatments.context_specific_role: MRSA-active treatment path for suspected or confirmed resistant gram-positive septic arthritis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Culture and susceptibility need to support activity against the true organism.
Gram-negative coverage matters with urinary, GI, healthcare, immunosuppressed, bite, or prosthetic contexts.
Anaerobic or Cutibacterium disease requires agents active against slow-growing anaerobes.

side_effects.interpretation: Some gram-negative regimens require renal adjustment or can be nephrotoxic.

treatments.context_specific_role: Culture-directed non-staphylococcal therapy after microbiology or epidemiologic context clarifies organism group.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Gonococcal arthritis follows a different microbiologic probability than S. aureus or prosthetic infection.
Cephalosporin effect depends on organism susceptibility and correct diagnosis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Antimicrobial path when disseminated gonococcal arthritis probability or mucosal evidence is high.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Aspiration works when there is accessible fluid to remove.
Aspiration alone rarely controls established prosthetic biofilm.

side_effects.interpretation: The procedure itself creates a recent joint instrumentation context.

treatments.context_specific_role: Drainage path for accessible native joint effusion, often repeated while antibiotics sterilize the joint.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Operative washout is source control when pus, loculation, deep joint, or inadequate aspiration exists.
Prosthetic infection often requires implant-specific surgical strategy rather than simple native-joint washout.

side_effects.interpretation: Perioperative instability and nephrotoxic exposures can add AKI risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Operative washout and debridement for purulent native joint infection or failed aspiration.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: This pathway exists only when prosthetic material is present.
Debridement with retention needs active antimicrobial suppression of retained biofilm.
Sinus tract or chronic drainage suggests mature biofilm and soft tissue failure.

side_effects.interpretation: Retained infected hardware can relapse and cause later functional loss if control fails.

treatments.context_specific_role: Implant-retention source-control path for selected prosthetic joint infections with manageable biofilm and active antibiotics.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Established biofilm is better controlled when infected material is removed.
Loose or failed implant makes retention less effective.

side_effects.interpretation: Staged revision and spacer periods can reduce function even while improving infection control.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control path when retained prosthetic material is unlikely to be sterilized.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage benefit is greatest when a deep collection is present.
Bone involvement often requires debridement plus longer active therapy.

side_effects.interpretation: Extensive debridement can sacrifice tissue while controlling infection.

treatments.context_specific_role: Control of abscess, osteomyelitis, mediastinal, iliopsoas, or other deep extension connected to the infected joint.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Removing an infected catheter or controlling endovascular source reduces recurrent seeding.
Remote source control matters most when bacteremia is present or likely.

treatments.context_specific_role: Control of a dialysis catheter, central line, skin abscess, urinary source, endocarditis source, or other remote driver of joint seeding.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluids improve circulating volume in septic hypoperfusion.
Renal failure or volume overload requires close reassessment.

side_effects.interpretation: Over-resuscitation can worsen oxygenation through pulmonary edema.

treatments.context_specific_role: Hemodynamic support while antibiotics and source control address the causal infection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressor effect is relevant when hypotension persists after volume assessment.
Perfusion support does not sterilize the joint or remove infected hardware.

side_effects.interpretation: Catecholamine exposure can add to lactate signal even as perfusion improves.

treatments.context_specific_role: Perfusion support for septic shock physiology from joint infection or associated bacteremia.

present.trajectory_modulation: Damaged or inflamed joints are more susceptible to seeding and can obscure early diagnosis.
Raises biofilm, sinus tract, need for implant-specific source control, relapse, and prolonged therapy.
Raises direct inoculation probability and can change organism spectrum toward skin flora, oral flora, gram-negative organisms, or anaerobes depending on exposure.
Raises hematogenous seeding, bacteremia, endocarditis hazard, and metastatic infection.
Raises catheter-source bacteremia, S. aureus probability, polyarticular disease, endocarditis hazard, and recurrent seeding unless the source is controlled.
Raises infection risk, severity, atypical presentation, gram-negative or opportunistic spectrum, procedure risk, and mortality.

over_65.trajectory_modulation: Raises bacteremia, prosthetic infection, atypical presentation, delayed diagnosis, functional loss, and mortality.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises hematogenous seeding, S. aureus or gram-negative probability, sternoclavicular or axial involvement, bacteremia, and endocarditis hazard.
Raises gonococcal probability and shifts presentation toward migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and lower bacteremia mortality than S. aureus septic shock.
Raises gram-negative, anaerobic, Pasteurella, Salmonella, or polymicrobial probabilities and changes empiric coverage needs.
Sustains intra-articular burden, raises cartilage destruction, abscess, bacteremia, functional loss, and mortality.

supportive_care: Obtain blood cultures and aspirate or operative joint samples for Gram stain, cell count, crystals, aerobic and anaerobic culture, and susceptibility when feasible without delaying therapy in unstable patients.
Do not treat a positive crystal result as excluding infection when bacterial arthritis remains clinically plausible.

Use ultrasound, CT, or MRI to identify effusion, deep joint involvement, abscess, osteomyelitis, prosthetic complications, sternoclavicular chest wall or mediastinal extension, or sacroiliac iliopsoas extension.
Start active antibacterial therapy promptly after cultures when feasible; in shock or rapidly progressive disease, do not delay therapy for difficult aspiration.
Reassess drainage adequacy when fever, bacteremia, pain, swelling, CRP, or effusion persist after 24-72 hours of active therapy.

Evaluate for bacteremia source and metastatic infection when blood cultures are positive, especially with S. aureus, multiple joints, dialysis catheter, prosthetic joint, embolic signs, or persistent fever.
Use echocardiography when S. aureus bacteremia, persistent bacteremia, embolic findings, prosthetic material, dialysis catheter, injection drug use, or new murmur raises endocarditis concern.

Coordinate orthopedics, infectious diseases, interventional radiology, and source-specific teams early for prosthetic joints, hip, shoulder, sternoclavicular, sacroiliac, spine-adjacent, polyarticular, or bacteremic disease.
Adjust antimicrobial dosing for kidney function and dialysis; monitor vancomycin exposure, renal function, cytopenias, and drug interactions.
Provide analgesia, splinting only briefly when needed for pain, early range-of-motion rehabilitation after infection control, venous thromboembolism prevention when safe, and glycemic optimization.
For prosthetic infection, document implant age, stability, sinus tract, organism, susceptibilities, bacteremia status, soft-tissue envelope, and surgical source-control plan.
Trend temperature, heart rate, MAP, oxygenation, WBC, CRP, ESR, creatinine, lactate when severe, blood culture clearance when positive, and joint function over time.
